name: Cornflower
lede: Cornflower is the blue of the grain-field weed Centaurea cyanus, a bright blue with a little violet in it, and since the X11 color list it has been a stock screen color.

sections.title: The flower and the word
sections.body:
Cornflower names the blue of *Centaurea cyanus*, a flower of the grain fields [1][2]. The French call it *bleuet*, and English borrowed the word as a color name too: Paterson defines *bluet* as the blue of the cornflower [3]. The writer Maggie Nelson recounts learning that *les bluets* can mean cornflowers, a flower she had thought she had never seen, though she had long used the word as her book's title [4].

Paterson also records the screen version: Cornflower Blue is one of the 140 colors of the X11 set, with the hex code #6495ED [5]. St Clair's glossary describes the shade as a bright blue with a little violet [6]. That matches the swatch here, which is a clear mid blue leaning toward violet [[periwinkle]] and away from the greener [[sky-blue]] [7].

sections.title: Where the name is recorded
sections.body:
In our library, Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color lists cornflower as first recorded in 1891, on plate 42 [7]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 puts the same hue in its block 194 [7]. In Google Books, its use as a color word peaks in the 2010s [8].

The nearest named blues on the screen are [[blue-grey]], [[clear-cadet-blue]], [[clear-cadet-blue]] and [[dodger-blue]], each within about five to six units of CIEDE2000 [7]. [[berlin-blue]] and [[lupine]] are slightly farther, at about seven [7].

sections.title: A flower in old blue vocabulary
sections.body:
Pastoureau notes that Greek and Roman writers described blue flowers, the cornflower among them, with words for red, green or black [9]. The old claim that the Greeks could not see blue is a myth; the evidence is about vocabulary, which gave blue little attention, and not about eyesight [9].

A medieval puzzle also touches the flower. The cloth color *pers* meant the darkest and costliest blue in northern Europe, and its origin is unresolved [10]. Gage lists proposed sources that include late Latin *pressus*, the peach blossom, Persian lilac, and the blue-violet cornflower [10]. Books disagree here, because the derivation is a proposal by some scholars and not a settled fact [10].

sections.title: Boyle's blue
sections.body:
The seventeenth-century chemist Robert Boyle recommended a blue made from cornflower petals [11]. Eighteenth-century watercolor books took the color up under three names: cornflower blue, Boyle's blue and cyan blue [11]. Harley, cited in the Pigment Compendium, found no evidence that it was ever sold commercially, and a writer called Hoofnail attacked it in 1738 [11]. The petals owe their color to anthocyanin pigments such as cyanidin, which Schweppe lists among the extractable components [12].

Baty's catalogue of Werner's nomenclature illustrates the flower itself, using a 1737 botanical plate in which the petals show Werner's verditter blue [13]. The match is to the name in Werner's system, not to a pigment in the plate [13]. Cyanin, Paterson adds, is the blue coloring matter of violets, cornflower and other flowers [14].

sections.title: In stones and in words
sections.body:
Gem dealers borrow the flower too. Finlay records a Sri Lankan dealer who described a sapphire as blue like cornflowers with a little violet in it [15]. The trade has its own grading names, but the comparison shows how ordinary the flower is as a reference blue [15]. Compare the [[gem:sapphire|sapphire]] with the [[flower:cornflower|cornflower]] and the blue that leans violet is easy to see.

In writing, the flower is a small blue accent. The filmmaker Derek Jarman lists a self-sown cornflower among the blues of his garden, beside bugloss and sage [16]. St Clair also notes that Quimper blue is a soft cornflower shade, the color of dusk [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 19 hold cornflower blue over at least five per cent of the canvas, within six units of CIEDE2000 [17]. That is about eight in ten thousand paintings [17]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test [17].

None of the 19 dates from before 1600, and the earliest, a Guercino of 1617, covers a small part of its canvas [17]. In the 1900s the color appears 3.7 times as often as expected [17]. [[painter:henri-matisse|Matisse]] is the standout: three of the 50 works here are matches, a rate about 75 times the baseline [17]. In a painting it plays a mid-tone about four times in five, and a highlight otherwise [17].

The Greeks could not see the color blue, which is why they rarely named it.
In our archive, which painter's work holds cornflower blue far more often than the museums' baseline?

openers: Cornflower blue was a real eighteenth-century watercolor name, made from petals, and Harley found no evidence it was ever sold commercially.
Look at a cornflower and notice the little violet in the blue: that lean is what separates it from sky blue.
Henri Matisse uses this blue far more than his museums' average, in three of the 50 works we hold.
